The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, apologies that curdled into silence, jokes that died on the vine. There's one to my mother from three years ago. "Mom, I know you're worried about—" and then nothing. I don't know what I was going to say. I still don't.

We think we're so connected now, don't we? The world at our fingertips, every voice reachable in seconds. But I've noticed something. The more ways we have to speak, the less we actually say. Or maybe that's just me. Maybe I'm the one who's broken.

My grandmother used to write letters. Real letters, with stamps and her careful cursive, the paper slightly yellowed from being held too long while she thought. She'd write to her sister in Ohio every Sunday. Forty years of Sundays. When she died, we found boxes of them. Her sister's replies, too. Two women talking about weather and grandchildren and the price of fabric, building a bridge across distance that I can't seem to cross with all my technology.

I tried to call my grandmother once, the last time I saw her. She was in the hospital, and I was in another state, and I thought—*I should call, I should say something important.* But I kept putting it off. "I'll call tomorrow," I told myself. "I'll find the right words." The right words never came. She died on a Tuesday. I still have her voicemail saved. Thirty seconds of her saying my name, the way only she could say it. I listen to it sometimes when I'm driving, when the road is long and empty and I need to feel less alone.

Here's what I've learned: the things we don't say don't disappear. They calcify. They become part of the architecture of who we are, these rooms we build with our silences. I have a friend I haven't spoken to in two years. We had a fight, or what I thought was a fight, some misunderstanding that grew teeth over text messages, over tone I misread, over pride I couldn't swallow. I drafted seventeen apologies. Deleted them all. Now I don't know how to start. The silence has become its own language, and I'm not fluent.

My therapist says I intellectualize my feelings. "You think about feeling instead of feeling," she said, and I laughed because it was true, because I was already analyzing why I laughed, what that revealed about my defense mechanisms. But sometimes I wonder if she's wrong. Maybe thinking *is* a kind of feeling. Maybe the problem isn't that I don't feel enough, but that I feel too much and thinking is how I survive it.

I read somewhere that the average person speaks 16,000 words a day. I don't believe I hit that. Some days I speak to three people. The barista. My neighbor, briefly. A customer service representative whose name I forget immediately. The rest of my words go into this—into writing, into thinking, into the drafts folder, into conversations I have with myself in the shower, rehearsing arguments I'll never have, speeches I'll never give.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver I keep returning to. "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" I used to find it inspiring. Now I find it terrifying. Because I don't know. I don't know what I'm doing with this life, this one wild and precious thing, and the not-knowing feels like a kind of failure. But maybe that's the point. Maybe the question is the answer, the asking itself the only response that matters.

I want to be braver with my words. I want to send the messages, make the calls, say the true thing even when my voice shakes. I want to stop building rooms out of silence. But bravery, I'm learning, isn't the absence of fear. It's fear plus action, fear and the doing anyway. So here's my action, small and ridiculous: I'm going to text my friend tonight. Not an apology, not a grand gesture. Just: "I miss you. Can we talk?"

Maybe she'll say yes. Maybe she won't. Maybe she's been waiting for me to reach out, or maybe she's moved on, built her own rooms, filled them with other people. Either way, I'll have tried. I'll have spoken into the silence and let it echo back, whatever it echoes.

The drafts folder stays. Some things need to stay unsaid, I think. Some words are for us alone, practice for the real thing, or memorials to who we were when we wrote them. But I'm done letting it be a graveyard. I want it to be a garden. Things growing, even if they never bloom.

1000 words, more or less. Whatever came.
